places.shortDescription: Khiva's tallest minaret (56.6–57 m) and compact 42-hujra madrasah, celebrated for alternating unglazed brick and turquoise tile bands.

localizedShortDescriptions.en: Khiva's tallest minaret (56.6–57 m) and compact 42-hujra madrasah, celebrated for alternating unglazed brick and turquoise tile bands.

localizedShortDescriptions.ru: Самый высокий минарет Хивы (56,6–57 м) и медресе на 42 худжры, знаменитые чередованием кирпича и бирюзовых изразцовых поясов.
localizedShortDescriptions.ja: 高さ約56.6〜57mを誇るヒヴァ最高のミナレットと42室のマドラサ複合施設。素焼きレンガとターコイズタイルの帯模様が特徴です。

localizedShortDescriptions.es: El minarete más alto de Jiva (56,6–57 m) junto a una madraza de 42 celdas, famoso por sus franjas horizontales de cerámica turquesa.

historicalFacts: Constructed between 1908 and 1910 at the initiative of Islam Khoja, the progressive Grand Vizier of the Khiva Khanate under Asfandiyar Khan.
Standing roughly 56.6 to 57 meters high, it is the tallest monument in Khiva and ranks among the tallest historic minarets in Central Asia.
Its upper viewing platform sits at approximately 45 meters and offers a panoramic view over all of Ichan-Qala and Dishan-Qala.
The adjacent madrasah is small yet finely proportioned, featuring 42 student cells (hujras) and a domed central hall.
architecturalDetails: The shaft tapers steeply upward like early medieval towers, visually accentuating its dramatic height.
Horizontal ornamental bands alternate warm baked brick with bright turquoise, white, and cobalt glazed ceramic tiles.
A narrow internal spiral staircase of stone/brick steps leads up to the lantern gallery.
localLegends: Cultural Tradition: Islam Khoja is remembered in Khiva as a modernizer who championed secular schools, telegraph lines, a hospital, and wider bridges before his assassination in 1913; the minaret became a lasting symbol of his legacy.
visualCues: Tallest slender brick minaret rising above Khiva's mudbrick skyline
Alternating horizontal rings of bright turquoise-white glazed tiles and plain tan brick
Open arched lantern cupola near the summit above a flared decorative cornice
Compact single-story madrasah facade directly attached to the minaret base

historicalFacts: Planned in the 1890s because Ichan-Qala lacked space for a new garden-palace, construction began in 1904 under Muhammad Rahim Khan II for his son Asfandiyar Khan.
After Muhammad Rahim Khan II's death in 1910, Asfandiyar Khan expanded the complex through 1912 as his official ceremonial reception hall.
Both Khivan masters and specialists from Russia and Germany contributed to the palace's hybrid architectural design and materials.
Its rooms feature Russian glazed ceramic tile fireplaces, European parquet flooring, crystal chandeliers, and Venetian mirrors.
architecturalDetails: Primary one-story palace buildings stand about 7.5 meters tall, arranged around enclosed inner courtyards and high brick perimeter walls.
Wooden carved columns, painted ceilings, and intricate ganch plasterwork sit side-by-side with arched European-style windows and stoves.
localLegends: Documented Naming Story: The site belonged to a wealthy merchant named Nurullaboy, who agreed to sell his orchard to the Khan only on condition that the new palace permanently bear his name.

historicalFacts: Erected in 1834–1835 by order and funds of Allakuli Khan on the line of Ichan-Qala's eastern wall beside his caravanserai and covered market.
The madrasah spans roughly 62.5 × 47 meters with 99 student hujras (90 in some counts), winter and summer mosques, and a lecture hall (darskhana).
A large library (kitabkhana) above the entrance served students from every madrasah across Khiva.
Inscribed as part of UNESCO World Heritage site Itchan Kala in 1990; today it houses the Abu Ali ibn Sina Museum of Medical History.
architecturalDetails: Built atop a ~3-meter raised artificial mound so its facade towers prominently over surrounding roofs.

Its portal faces the courtyard of the older Khojamberdibiy Madrasah in the Central Asian 'kosh' (paired) layout; because of the irregular junction, Khojamberdibiy gained the nickname 'Khurjum' (saddlebag).
Exterior portal and courtyard iwans are richly clad in classic Khorezmian black, white, and blue-turquoise majolica, whereas student cells inside were left smoothly plastered in plain ganch.
localLegends: Historical Architectural Context: Cutting the madrasah straight into the eastern fortress wall forced builders to divide neighboring Khojamberdibiy Madrasah into two symmetrical halves, inspiring locals to call the complex 'Khurjum' (a woven double saddlebag).

historicalFacts: In 1851 Muhammad Amin Khan (reigned 1846–1855) held a design competition for a monumental madrasah and minaret; the plan by master Abdulla 'Jin' won approval.
Built between 1852 and 1855 (some sources note work started in 1851), it stands as the largest madrasah in Khiva with dimensions of roughly 78 × 60 meters.
Its 125 multi-room student hujras accommodated up to 260 scholars at a time, and also historically hosted the Khan's supreme court chamber.
Part of UNESCO World Heritage site Itchan Kala since 1990; today it operates as an exhibition space and tourist complex.
architecturalDetails: Two-story brick building topped by five domes and flanked by cylindrical corner towers (guldastas), with a portal rising ~25 meters.
Distinctive open arched balconies (loggias) run along the outer second-story facade—a rare structural touch among Central Asian madrasahs.
Historically connected on the second level to Kalta Minor Minaret via an arched wooden bridge.
localLegends: Craftsman Lore: Master tilemaker and architect Abdulla earned the nickname 'Abdulla Jin' ('Genie') because locals marveled at the extraordinary symmetry and gleaming turquoise ceramics he produced.
visualCues: Massive two-story tan-brick facade standing directly next to the turquoise Kalta Minor Minaret

historicalFacts: Construction began in 1871 by decree of Muhammad Rahim Khan II (reigned 1863–1910), an enlightened ruler and poet known by the pen name Feruz Shah.
Completed in 1876—three years after Khiva became a protectorate of the Russian Empire—it stands directly opposite Kunya-Ark's main eastern entrance.
Measuring 62 × 50 meters, it was the last large madrasah built in Khiva and housed 76 single-story cells designed for 152 students.
Poets including Komil Khorezmi composed celebratory chronogram verses commemorating its completion.
architecturalDetails: Rectangular complex enclosing a four-iwan courtyard with corner towers, winter and summer mosques, a classroom (darskhana), and a library.
Its monumental portal opens through a five-span arcade vestibule; student cells are roofed with traditional Balkhi domes.
localLegends: Literary Tradition: Khan Feruz actively cultivated music, lithography, and classical poetry in Khiva—today the madrasah also houses exhibits honoring Khorezmian literature and Feruz's cultural circle.

historicalFacts: Built around 1832–1833 under Allakuli Khan as part of an integrated commercial district beside his caravanserai and eastern Palvan-Darvoza gate.
Once the Tim and caravanserai opened, trade shifted from inside the neighboring Palvan-Darvoza corridor into these dedicated vaulted market halls.
The Khan invested customs and shop rent revenues from the Tim directly as waqf income supporting his new madrasah and public works.
architecturalDetails: Constructed from baked brick as an elongated gallery covered by a sequence of spherical domes with central roof oculus openings.
Thick masonry walls and high skylights naturally ventilated the bazaar and buffered 45°C summer desert heat.
localLegends: Trade Heritage: Merchants from Bukhara, Iran, and Russia traded silk, tea, carpets, and spices beneath these brick domes, and artisans still exhibit textiles and woodwork along its vaulted passage today.

historicalFacts: Rebuilt in baked brick in 1806 under Eltuzar Khan; its current form integrates modifications from 1832–1835 when Allakuli Khan built the Tim and madrasah.
Historically served as Khiva's primary city gate, guarded by a commander (mirshab) and seven armed guards (navkars), whose commander drew the same salary as the captain of the Khan's citadel.
A canal fed by the Amu Darya formed a defensive moat around the wall, crossed by a drawbridge raised each night.
architecturalDetails: Features an elongated multi-domed interior corridor (dolon) that originally housed small market stalls along its arched bays.
Twin flanking watchtowers project seamlessly from the city's outer defensive wall, allowing watchmen to survey approaches from the east.
localLegends: Folklore & Nicknames: Named 'Palvan-Darvoza' after Khiva's patron wrestler-poet Pahlavon Mahmud; earlier generations also grimly referred to it as 'Poshshob' (Executioner's) or 'Qul' (Slave) Gate because decrees and slave markets historically operated near the eastern approach.

In the 17th century a prayer/pilgrimage hall (ziaratkhona) was added onto the original tomb.
In 1825, Allakuli Khan ordered a major restoration of the monument.
architecturalDetails: Partially recessed relative to the raised modern street level due to centuries of surrounding urban buildup.

localLegends: Pilgrimage Tradition: Sayid Alauddin is honored locally as an early spiritual mentor in Khiva, and the shrine has remained a quiet place of reverence for seven centuries.

The outer pakhsa wall measured 6,250 meters long, 7 to 8 meters high, and 5 to 6 meters thick, originally pierced by 10 gates (of which Hazorasp and Qosh Gates still stand).
Khivan poet and historian Agahi recorded that Allakuli Khan mobilized over 200,000 workers—requiring subjects to contribute 12 days of unpaid labor—digging clay from Govukkol north of the city.
Monumental landmarks in Dishan-Kala include Nurullaboy Palace, Sayidboy Madrasah, Tort Shabbaz, and Abdolbobo complexes.
architecturalDetails: Built of rammed clay (pakhsa) and sun-dried mudbrick along wide radial avenues (Hazorasp, Bogi Shamol, Shohimardon, Qosh).
Traditional residential quarters preserve carved wooden ayvan verandas, clay courtyards, and craft workshops.
localLegends: Chronicle Note: Sources vary on construction speed—popular accounts speak of intense 6-week emergency mobilization, while Agahi's written chronicle describes 3 years of seasonal 12-day corvée labor.

historicalFacts: Meaning 'Big Yard' ('Uly Howly' in Turkmen), the fortified residential complex was built between 1640 and 1694 during the reign of scholar-ruler Abulghazi Bahadur Khan.
An inscription on the entrance gate records that Abulghazi Bahadur Khan ordered it built at the request of Salor Turkmen elders Khojamberdi and Shermamatboy.
Originally planned around a 100-room fortified compound housing 15 large extended families; 35 traditional living quarters survive today.
In 2009, scholars from the Khorezm Mamun Academy and Urgench State University conducted architectural studies here; it now welcomes visitors as an open-air Uzbek-Turkmen ethnographic complex.
architecturalDetails: Surrounded by tall rammed-earth (pakhsa) outer perimeter walls with defensive corner towers and a massive wooden double gate.
Interior courtyards preserve traditional clay homes, shaded wooden terraces, millstones, and yurt demonstration grounds.
localLegends: Shared Heritage: Referenced in the Khivan chronicle 'Firdavs ul-Iqbol' by Munis and Agahi, Ulli Hovli stands as a living monument to centuries of shared Uzbek and Turkmen brotherhood in the Khorezm oasis.

historicalFacts: Archaeological strata with ceramic finds and towered fortress walls date to the first half of the 1st millennium BCE, giving Hazorasp over 3,000 years of urban history.

Its Persian name 'Hazarasp' translates to 'Thousand Horses'; major medieval battles took place here involving Mahmud of Ghazni (1017), Seljuq Sultan Ahmad Sanjar vs. Khwarazmshah Atsiz (1147), and the Mongol invasion.
Later served as a stronghold for Arabshahid princes of Khiva and was captured during the 1873 Russian campaign.
Included on Uzbekistan's UNESCO World Heritage Tentative List.
architecturalDetails: Massive surviving earthen pakhsa ramparts and bastion ruins enclose a large quadrilateral citadel site beside historic irrigation canals.

historicalFacts: Consists of three interconnected ancient fortresses constructed between the 4th century BCE and the 7th century CE.
Ayaz-Kala 1 dates to the late 4th or early 3rd century BCE, built when Khorezm gained independence from Achaemenid Persia to guard oasis settlements from steppe nomad raids.
Sections of the complex (including Ayaz-Kala 2) were developed in the 2nd century CE during the Kushan period.
Administratively located in Ellikqala District (Karakalpakstan), right across the Amu Darya on the historic Khorezm oasis loop from Khiva.

The dish gained wider national recognition in 1958 when Khivan master chef Rajab Sattarov moved to Tashkent and shared the traditional recipe.
Recommended especially during hot Khorezm summers because the fresh dill herb and sour-milk suzma (chakka) provide vitamins, minerals, and cooling balance.
architecturalDetails: Fresh finely minced dill (or dill infusion) is kneaded directly into wheat noodle dough, giving boiled strands a bright emerald-green color.
